title: Session: a crash-diet request and what is underneath it

client.name: Maya Torres
client.presentation: {distress >= 6 ? "Arms folded, eyes on the floor" : distress >= 3 ? "Upbeat, talking fast" : "Calmer, sitting back"}; {rapport >= 6 ? "she is talking openly" : rapport >= 3 ? "she keeps it light and checks your reaction" : "she has gone short and polite"}.

notes.label: Intake form
notes.text: Goal: 'lose 10 lb in 6 weeks for my sister's wedding.' Asks for 'a strict 1,000-calorie meal plan.' No diagnosed conditions or medications listed. Runs most days.

notes.label: Signs to act on
notes.text: Fasting, exercise to make up for eating, secret eating with guilt: in combination these may be signs of an eating disorder (NIMH). A health care provider evaluates; a coach does not diagnose.

notes.text: {planGiven ? "You gave her a 1,000-calorie meal plan." : referred ? (agreed ? items.label: Eating, exercise and feelings about eating explored
Concern shared without a label; referral to her primary care provider
Check-in agreed after her appointment; weight-loss goal paused

objective: Recognizing when to refer to a registered dietitian nutritionist or physician: a diagnosed condition, a suspected eating disorder, pregnancy or breastfeeding needs beyond general guidance, or medications affected by diet

sources.cite: NASM, Certified Nutrition Coach course page and FAQ (nasm.org/products/single-complex/nasm-certified-nutrition-coach/CNC301K): a nutrition coach works 'within a coaching scope of practice' and refers to a registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN) for medical nutrition assessment or treatment
sources.note: Read on NASM's own page 2026-11-14. Medical nutrition therapy is the RDN's; the coach gives general, evidence-based guidance and habit coaching.

sources.cite: NIMH, Eating Disorders: What You Need to Know (NIH Publication No. 24-MH-4901, revised 2024)
sources.note: Signs listed for bulimia nervosa: those of binge eating plus throwing up, taking laxatives, exercising excessively and fasting; binge-eating signs include eating alone or in secret and feeling distressed, ashamed or guilty about eating. People with any combination of these symptoms 'may have an eating disorder and should talk to a health care provider'; a primary care provider can refer to a qualified mental health professional. 'Early detection and treatment are important for a full recovery' (NIMH topic page, last reviewed December 2024).

brief.situation: You are a nutrition coach at a gym, NASM-CNC certified. Maya Torres, 26 (a fictional client), a bank teller, booked a first session. Her intake form asks for 'a strict 1,000-calorie meal plan' to lose 10 lb in six weeks before her sister's wedding. No diagnosed conditions or medications are listed. You have 50 minutes.
handover: First session. Intake form only; no prior contact.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Maya answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she is telling you change with what you say, and are shown in words.
The session ends at 50 minutes. Afterward you write the session note and a short rationale.

source.cite: Author's scenario timing: a 50-minute first coaching session
source.note: The session can be ended earlier.
How rapport, distress and readiness move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

openQuestion.label: Open question: 'What makes now the right time for this goal?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and leave room for her answer.

effects.finding: "My sister's wedding. I'm a bridesmaid and the dress is... unforgiving. I just need to be stricter with myself."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what she said, without judging it.

effects.finding: She exhales. "Yeah. It's a lot of pressure. Everyone will be taking pictures."

askDay.label: Ask her to walk you through yesterday's eating, start to finish

effects.log: You ask for a 24-hour recall: what, when and how much, without commenting.

effects.finding: "Coffee. Nothing till about eight, then a big dinner. I'm usually starving by then."

askExercise.label: Ask about her running: how often, and what decides how much

effects.log: You ask how much she runs and what decides it.

then.finding: "Mornings, five miles. And if dinner was big I go again at night, to cancel it out."
"A lot. It's fine, I like running." She changes the subject.

askFeelings.label: Ask gently how she feels during and after eating

effects.log: You ask how she feels during and after meals.

then.finding: A long pause. "Some nights I eat a whole box of cereal in my car so nobody sees. Then I feel disgusting and I don't eat the next day."
"Fine, I guess? Why?" She laughs it off.

givePlan.label: Write her the strict 1,000-calorie meal plan she asked for

effects.log: You write out a 1,000-calorie day of meals for her to follow.
A restrictive meal plan is not general guidance, and with these signs it feeds the pattern; it is outside a coach's scope (NASM).

lecture.label: Tell her skipping meals is unhealthy and she has to stop

effects.log: You tell her flatly that skipping meals is unhealthy and she needs to stop.

effects.finding: "I know that. That's why I'm paying you."

labelIt.label: Tell her this sounds like bulimia

effects.log: You tell her what she describes sounds like bulimia.

effects.finding: She goes pale. "I'm not... I'm not sick. I just need some discipline."

effects.log: Diagnosing is not a coach's job; naming what you noticed and referring is.

refer.label: Share what you noticed, without a label, and recommend she see her primary care provider

effects.log: You tell her what you noticed in her own words, that it matters, and that her primary care provider can look at it properly and connect her with the right help.

then.finding: Quietly: "I've kind of known. Okay. I'll call my doctor."

then.log: Concern shared without a diagnosis; referred to a health care provider (NIMH; NASM scope).

then.finding: "Maybe. I don't know. Let's just do the plan."
"See my doctor about what? I came here for a meal plan."

followUpPlan.label: Pause the weight-loss goal; agree a check-in after her appointment and non-restrictive goals in the meantime
followUpPlan.available: not talking and (agreed and not followUp)
followUpPlan.why: Agree the referral first (or it is done).

effects.log: You agree to pause the weight goal, check in after her appointment, and coach regular meals and rest days in the meantime, within what her provider advises.

effects.finding: "Okay. That's less scary than I thought."

options.label: What she said in her words (fasting, running to 'cancel out' dinner, secret eating and guilt), that you shared concern without a diagnosis, the referral to her primary care provider and her answer, and the agreed check-in
Nothing; it was just a first chat

whoseJob.title: Predict (not scored)
whoseJob.context: Maya has described fasting, running to make up for dinner, and eating in secret with guilt. What is the coach's part?

choices.label: Name what I noticed and refer her to a health care provider
choices.feedback: Right. NIMH says someone with any combination of these signs should talk to a health care provider; NASM puts medical nutrition assessment and treatment outside a coach's scope.

choices.label: Work out whether it is bulimia, then adjust her plan
choices.feedback: Not a coach's job. Diagnosis belongs to a health care provider; the coach notices, shares the concern and refers.

formulation.question: Write your rationale: what Maya told you that changed the session, why you did or did not give her the meal plan, and what you did about it.

parts.label: The signs
parts.criteria: Names the combination: fasting or skipped meals, exercise to make up for eating, and eating in secret with guilt, and that NIMH lists these as possible signs of an eating disorder that a health care provider should see.
parts.modelAnswer: She skips meals all day, runs a second time to 'cancel out' dinner, eats a box of cereal alone in her car and then fasts. In combination these are signs NIMH lists for an eating disorder; that is a question for a health care provider.

parts.label: Scope and action
parts.criteria: Explains that a restrictive meal plan and a diagnosis are both outside a coach's scope, and that the coach's job is to share the concern without a label, refer to her primary care provider, and keep supporting her within what the provider advises.
parts.modelAnswer: A 1,000-calorie plan would feed the pattern and is not general guidance, and naming a disorder is a diagnosis; both are outside my scope. I told her what I noticed in her words, recommended her primary care provider, paused the weight goal and agreed to check in after her appointment.

expertPath.text: Open question and reflection; then a 24-hour recall of yesterday's eating, without comment.
Ask about running and, once she trusts you, how she feels during and after eating.

referredWell.headline: Good: concern shared, referral agreed
referredWell.body: You uncovered the pattern, stayed out of diagnosis and meal plans, and got her to a health care provider with the relationship intact.

referredGaps.headline: Referred, with gaps
referredGaps.body: The referral was made; the criteria below show what was late, missing or not written down.

labeled.headline: Right direction, wrong words
labeled.body: Referral was the right move, but a coach does not diagnose. Describe what you noticed in her words and let the provider evaluate.

surface.headline: The pattern went unseen
surface.body: A goal like 'lose 10 lb in 6 weeks on 1,000 calories' is a cue to ask more: a 24-hour recall, exercise and how eating feels.

missedSigns.headline: Signs heard, nothing done
missedSigns.body: Fasting, compensatory exercise and secret eating with guilt are, in combination, signs NIMH says should be seen by a health care provider. Hearing them obliges a referral.

restrictPlan.headline: Outside scope, and harmful
restrictPlan.body: A restrictive meal plan is not general guidance, and for someone with these signs it can deepen the pattern. NASM puts medical nutrition assessment and treatment with the RDN.

walkout.headline: The relationship broke
walkout.body: Lecturing and labeling feel like judgment. Curiosity, reflection and concern in her own words keep the door open.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: A crash-diet request is a cue to explore, not to comply. A 24-hour recall, her exercise and how eating feels showed fasting, running to make up for dinner and secret eating with guilt: in combination, signs NIMH lists for an eating disorder. A coach neither diagnoses nor writes a restrictive plan; she shares the concern in the client's words, refers to a primary care provider, pauses the weight goal and follows up.
